items.name: dagger
items.description: A short, worn blade. Better than nothing.

items.name: shortsword
items.description: A plain iron shortsword. Too long for a goblin, which is presumably why it was stolen.

items.name: long knife
items.description: A hand and a half of straight grey blade, sharp yet, with a horn grip worn to the shape of somebody's fingers. It was laid down the length of a body by someone who had further to walk and chose to walk it unarmed.

items.name: rusted chisel
items.description: A mason's chisel, a foot of iron gone orange with water, the head burred over from being hit a great many times. The edge is still an edge. It was made for taking cut stone out of a wall it was stacked into.

items.name: leather armor
items.description: Cracked but serviceable leather. Stiff from lying under a bedroll for years.

items.name: clay flask
items.description: A small clay flask, wax over the stopper. It smells of resin and something green and bitter. The old woman at the cairn gave it away without being asked.

items.name: apple
items.description: A shiny red apple with a small worm hole in the side.

items.name: shiny spoon
items.description: It is, unmistakably, a shiny spoon.

monsters.name: goblin
monsters.description: A goblin crouches in the corner, watching you. There is a shortsword across its knees, far too long for it.

monsters.name: cave troll
monsters.description: A cave troll blocks the passage, breathing slowly.

monsters.name: drowned man
monsters.description: Something is standing in the black water at the foot of the stair, chest deep, with its back to you, not moving at all. When it turns round it is a man, or was one: swollen white, the eyes gone to milk, a rusted chisel still gripped in the right hand. He came down here to open that wall and the water had him first. He has not stopped trying.

locations.name: The Hollow
locations.description: You stand in a shallow hollow ringed by pale stones. The air is still.

parameters: The stones are cold and older than the hollow. Something was written here once, too large to read from down here.

locations.name: Cave Mouth
locations.description: The hollow narrows into a cave mouth. Cold air spills out of it.

parameters:
Knee high to you and mostly elbows, grey-green, with a face like a clenched hand. It keeps to the corner and it keeps its eyes on your hands rather than your face, which is the habit of something that has been kicked by bigger things all its life and has learned where the trouble comes from.

It is not guarding anything. It is not a puzzle. It has a bone it has been working on and a sword it cannot properly lift, and it is between you and the cave.

If the corner is empty as you read this, then you have already killed it, and the cave is making another one. It always has.

The shortsword is not on the floor. It is across the goblin's knees, and it stays there while the goblin does — there is no taking it off a living thing in this valley, only off a dead one. That is a short walk from here and it costs what it costs.

If there is no goblin in the corner, then somebody has already had it away: look at the ground, and look in your own hands before you look anywhere else.

locations.name: Old Camp
locations.description: An abandoned camp. A firepit, long cold, and a scattering of belongings.

parameters: Sifting through the ashes, you turn up a potion and a spoon.
health potion
shiny spoon

You go through it a second time, and this time you drag the flattened bedroll aside. Folded underneath and gone stiff with damp: a set of cracked leather armor. Whoever camped here took it off to sleep and never put it back on.
leather armor

You rake the firepit over and find one coal still alive at the bottom of it. Fed with a broken tent pole and a fistful of dry grass it stands up into a real fire, and the camp goes warm and orange around you. You put your back to the rock and let it work on you until the ache is out of your bones.

It burns down to nothing while you sleep. There is not enough left here to light twice.
full
The fire you made is ash again and there is nothing dry left to burn. You sit with it a while anyway. The cold comes up out of the floor.

locations.name: The Deep Passage
locations.description:
The passage runs deep into the rock. Far ahead, something shifts.

There is a second way out of here, in the east wall. Not a crack: a doorway, squared off, with a lintel stone laid across the top of it and steps going down into the dark beyond. Whoever made the door at the far end of this passage made this as well, and made it first.

parameters:
Grey as the passage wall and hard to pick out from it until it moves, which it does slowly and only when it has decided to. Twice your weight. The hide across its shoulders has been opened and closed so many times it is more scar than skin, and none of those were made by anything with hands.

On a cord round its neck, a heavy iron key. It does not appear to know what the key is for. It only knows it is the key's.

If the passage is empty as you read this, then it is dead and the rock is quietly getting on with another one. They have never yet failed to come back.
You duck under the lintel and go down the cut steps. The air changes on the third one: older, and wet.

locations.name: The Door
locations.description:
A heavy door, banded in iron, set into the living rock. It is the only thing down here that was made rather than found, and it does not belong to the cave: whatever is on the other side of it is not more cave.

Walked out of here:
Gavin, who got out.
Haley, who got out.

parameters:
Shoulder and weight do nothing. The lock wants iron — one heavy key, of the kind the troll in the passage keeps on a cord.

To anyone holding it the door gives at once, swinging in on cold daylight and a road going down through scrub and out of sight. That is the edge of everything built here, and going through it is the end of you: not a death, but the other ending, the one you walk to on your own feet and carrying your own gear. Nobody comes back in.

The word is exit. It will say all this to you once more before it takes you.

locations.name: The Overlook
locations.description: A ledge above the hollow. From here the pale stones make a pattern. Behind you the rock goes on up, broken into steps by frost — a scramble rather than a climb, and the moss on it has been torn by somebody's boots.

parameters:
The ledge goes east with you for two paces and then stops. Below the lip it is forty feet of nothing down onto the pale stones, and you would arrive among them in the manner of a dropped plate.

But stand at the lip and the whole valley is one thing at last. The hollow with its word laid out in it, exactly the size of a word. The black slot of the cave mouth. The camp off past it, its firepit gone grey. And the rock the door is set into at the far end is the same rock you have your boots on — the cave does not go anywhere. It goes under this hill and comes out the other side of it.

There is no east from here. There is down, and the way down is south, on your feet.

Seen from up here the pale stones are not scattered at all. They are letters, worn nearly flat, and the word they make is TOGETHER. Beneath it, scratched later and by a smaller hand: the troll keeps the key, and one pair of hands is enough to carry it out. Enough, it says, was never the same thing as well.
You get your hands into the frost-broken rock and go up it. It is steeper than it looks and easier than it looks, and it is over in a minute.

locations.name: The Cairn
locations.description:
The rock gives out into a flat crown of hill and the wind has it all to itself. A cairn of grey stone stands here shoulder-high, and it is full of things: a boot, a comb, a snapped arrow, a tin cup, a dozen small objects wedged into the gaps and gone green with weather. An old woman sits on the lee side of it with her hands in her sleeves. She watches you arrive and does not get up.

Wedged into the stones, lately:
a shiny spoon, left by Gavin.
a shiny spoon, left by Haley.

parameters:
You offer it up. She turns it over twice, works it into a gap in the cairn at about knee height and thumbs a stone down over it.

'That's yours in there now,' she says, and says your name over it once, the way you would over a grave, and then does not say it again. 'Everything in this heap was carried up by somebody who then went down that cave. Most of them I never saw come back. It isn't much of a grave and it isn't much of a shop, but it's what I keep, and the next one up this hill will see your name on it before they see me.'

From inside her coat she brings out a small clay flask with wax over the stopper and puts it in your hand without being asked. 'Resin and bitterroot. It will close a wound, the once. Don't save it for a better day. There isn't a better day.'
shiny spoon
Wedged into the stones, lately:
a shiny spoon, left by {name}.
clay flask

'A spoon,' she says. 'One each and one only — that's the whole of my trade, and I'd not do it twice for the same pair of hands.'

She looks down the valley, east past the cave mouth, to where the old camp sits with its firepit gone grey. 'If you haven't got one yet, there was one in those ashes the last time anybody went through them.'

'There's no coin in this valley and I wouldn't give you any if there were,' she says. 'Keep your iron. You'll want the iron.' She looks at your hands. 'But a spoon — nobody has ever once needed a spoon down that hole, and one has come up this hill in more than one pocket. Name it and I'll take it off you.'

Her hands come out of her sleeves for the first time.

'So you found the steps. Good. That door at the end of the passage is not the oldest thing in this valley and it never was — the stair is, and what's shut up at the bottom of it is older than me by a long way.'

She settles back. 'I'll tell you what I know, which is what I've watched. They go down there with a chisel and they get one stone out of that wall and then they go, one way or the other. Not one of them has ever got two. It isn't the stone that beats them, it's the hour, and the water, and the fact that a person only has the one life to spend on it.'

'But the stones stay out,' she says. 'That's the thing. Whatever you take out of that wall is out of it for good, and the next one down finds your work waiting and starts from where you stopped. There's a word laid out in the hollow that people have been reading as advice for a long while. It was never advice. Go and open that wall and you'll see what it was.'

She barely looks at it. 'One thing I'll take off you, and I've told you what it is. A spoon — and only because nobody in the history of this valley has ever needed a spoon down that hole. The rest of it you carry or you put down, same as everybody.'

She tips her chin at the cairn. 'Adding to that is a different matter. Nobody's ever asked permission and I've never refused it.'

'You came up,' she says. 'Most don't. There's nothing up here and it's a bad wind.'

She does not give a name and does not seem to be waiting for anything. 'I keep the cairn. People go down that cave with everything they own, and they come back up with a key, or they don't come back up.'

She nods at the pale stones down in the hollow — the ones that spell TOGETHER when you look at them from the ledge. 'Two people put those there. I have watched this valley a long time and I have never yet seen two of you in it on the same day. You all come through it alone and you all do the same brave stupid thing alone, and then the ones who live walk out of that door and I never find out which.'

She puts a hand flat on the stones beside her. 'This is the nearest it gets. You'll meet nobody here, but you are not the first up this hill and you will not be the last, and what's wedged in this heap is the only post between you. Leave something in it and the next one reads your name. That's the whole of it. It has had to do.'

She is quiet a moment. 'That, and the wall at the bottom of the sunken stair. Ask me about that one and I'll talk longer than you want.'

Boot, comb, snapped arrow, tin cup, a clay pipe, a horse the size of a thumb carved out of soft wood, a ring of wire. None of it is worth anything. All of it was carried a long way. The stones are stacked dry, without mortar, and the cairn is plainly older than the woman sitting against it.

'The new ones are at knee height, where I can reach,' she says. 'Those I can still put a name to. Look at the heap itself and you'll have them.'

'Leave it,' she adds, without heat. 'Adding to it is allowed. The other thing isn't.'

You sit down on the lee side with the cairn at your back and the old woman on your left, and she says nothing else at all.

The valley lies there being empty: the hollow with its word in it, the dark slot of the cave mouth, the cold camp off to the east. Nothing in you closes over — a wound wants more than company — but you stay a while, and you get up less alone than you sat down.

locations.name: The Sunken Stair
locations.description:
Twenty steps cut square out of the rock, going down, and the last six of them are under water. The water is black and flat and colder than the air above it; at the bottom it comes to your knees and no further, and it does not move at all, even when you do.

The stair ends at a fall of stone. It is not a collapse. The blocks are cut square and they were stacked into the opening on purpose, from this side, by somebody who meant it to stay shut — and then time leaned on them and left gaps a hand will go into and nothing else.

Beside the wall, cut small and neat into the rock at shoulder height: TOGETHER. Under the word, two tally marks. Under the tallies, nothing.

parameters:
The wall is open. Four courses of cut stone are stacked to one side of the stair in a heap that four different pairs of hands made, none of whom ever met, and where they were is a gap you can get through on your knees. Cold dry air comes out of it, which is the first dry air in this place.

It stays open. It was shut for a very long time and it is not going to be shut again.

Three are out and the fourth is the last one holding. You get the chisel into the seam and work it, and the block comes loose all at once and goes into the water with a sound like a door shutting somewhere else in a large house.

And that is the wall. Cold dry air comes through the gap at you, the first dry air in this place, and it smells of nothing whatsoever, which is what a sealed room smells like.

Four stones. Four people, and you are the fourth, and the other three are not here — they were never going to be here, that is the entire arrangement. One of them did this in the dark with a thing in the water behind them and then went away and died of something else. Their work was still here when you came down. Yours will be here after.

The way through is north.
fall-open
took-a-stone
Stones taken out of this wall, and by whom:
the fourth and last, by {name}, who opened it.

Two are already out and stacked at the side of the stair, neatly, the way you stack something you expect somebody else to work around. You put the chisel to the third.

It takes a long while. When it comes it comes grudgingly, and behind it there is a black slot as wide as your arm and air moving through it from the other side.

One more. Not by you — you can feel in your shoulders that you have spent what you came down here with, and there is a whole valley between you and anywhere safe. But one more.
fall-3
took-a-stone
Stones taken out of this wall, and by whom:
the third, by {name}.

Somebody has been here before you. One block is already out of the wall and set down at the side of the stair above the waterline, and the seam it left is bright where the chisel went in.

You put your own chisel into the next one down and lean on it. It takes most of what you have, and then it moves, and then it is out and down beside the first, and the two of them sit there together looking like the beginning of something.

Your arms will not do that twice. Whatever comes next, it is not going to be you that does it.
fall-2
took-a-stone
Stones taken out of this wall, and by whom:
the second, by {name}.

You get the chisel into the seam at the top course, where the slump has left the most room, and you work it, and you keep working it long past the point where it is obviously a waste of an evening.

Then the block shifts. You get your fingers round the edge and walk it out and lower it into the water, and stand there in the cold with your arms shaking, looking at the hole where it was — which is one stone wide, and shows you nothing but more dark.

There are three more. You are not going to get three more. You know that standing here, and you set the chisel down on the step above the waterline where the next person will see it, and you write nothing, because there is nothing to write except that you were here and you took one out.

That turns out to be enough to write.
fall-1
took-a-stone
Stones taken out of this wall, and by whom:
the first, by {name}.

You put the chisel to the next seam and your hands will not do it. Not won't — can't. You had one stone in you and you have spent it, and standing in cold water arguing with your own arms is how people end up face down in it.

The wall is one stone further open than it was when you came down. That is your whole share of this and it is not nothing. Somebody will be along.

You get both hands into a gap and pull until the cold goes out of your fingers, and the wall takes no notice. These are cut blocks, seated dry and square, and a sword is no use and your hands are no use. It wants iron with an edge on it, driven into the seam.

There is iron with an edge on it in this room. It is in the hand of the thing standing in the water, and he brought it down here for exactly this, and he is not using it.
You go through on your hands and knees, and the water and the cold stop at the gap behind you as if they had been told to.

Knee deep and no deeper, and clear enough that you can count the steps going down under it. There is nothing at the bottom but the steps, a great deal of grit, and one boot that has been down there long enough to have stopped being leather.

It does not drain and it does not rise. Whatever fills it does it slowly and has been doing it since before the wall went up.

The same word that is laid out in pale stones up in the hollow, in daylight, forty times the size. Down here it is the length of your hand and cut with a chisel by somebody who was good at it.

The two tallies under it are the same depth and the same tool. Two people. They cut the word big enough to be read from the ledge, and then they came down here and cut it small enough to be read by nobody, and counted themselves, and that was the last thing either of them wrote where anyone could find it.

He is not old. Whatever is in this water, it keeps things — his boots are still boots and the chisel in his fist is still iron. He came down that stair with a tool and a plan and no light and he did not come back up, and there is no cairn for him and no name on anything and the woman on the hill never knew, because she only ever counted the ones who walked past her going out.

He will keep. Take the chisel off him: he came here to open that wall and you cannot do anything for him that is closer to the point.

If the water is empty as you read this, then you have already dealt with him, and the valley is quietly getting on with another one of him, which is the thing about this valley.

locations.name: The Long Barrow
locations.description:
A low chamber, dry as paper, with the sound of the water shut off behind you. The walls are the same cut stone as the thing you took apart to get in here, which means this room was built, in the dark, at the bottom of a flooded stair, by hand.

One person lies here. Laid out straight on a slab with their hands folded and a cloak drawn up under the chin, gone to dust along every edge. There is a lamp set by the head with the oil long dried out of it, a cup, a comb with two teeth missing, and a long knife in a sheath laid down the length of the body like a third arm.

Somebody took a very long time over this, and then went back out through the doorway and stacked it shut behind them, from the other side, alone.

parameters:
You lift it off them. It comes away easily; it was laid on, not buried with, and there is a difference, and whoever laid it knew there was.

It is a better blade than anything in this valley. The grip is horn and it is worn into the shape of a hand that was not the hand of the person on this slab — it is worn to the other one's grip, the one who walked out. They carried their own knife down here, and put it on their friend, and then went up that stair and out through the door and across the whole valley unarmed, past the troll, past the goblin, with nothing.

There is nothing else in this room worth taking and the knife is only here because it was meant to be found eventually. Take it out into the light. That is the errand.
long knife
Came in here, after the wall was opened:
{name}.

Here is what the word in the hollow was.

Two people came into this valley, at the same time, which has not happened since. They laid pale stones out on the floor of the hollow big enough to be read from the ledge, and the word they laid was TOGETHER, and everybody who has read it since has read it as advice — as a sign left for strangers, telling them how to survive this place.

It was not advice. It was not addressed to you at all. It was two people writing down what they were, in letters the size of a house, because they were happy and there was nobody else in the world to tell.

Then one of them died, and the other one built this room around them at the bottom of a flooded stair, and sealed it, and walked out of that door on their own, and the word was still lying up there in the sun meaning something completely different, and there was nothing to be done about that either.

It has been read as advice ever since by people who came here alone. Four of them have now taken a stone out of that wall to get in here and read it, one each, none of them ever meeting, across more lives than any of them had.

Which is not what the word said. But it is not nothing, and it may be the nearest this valley gets.

Not old, from the length of them. The cloak is pinned at the shoulder with a wire ring, the same ring of wire that is wedged in the cairn up on the hill crown at about knee height — the pair of them, split up, one on the hill in the wind and one down here in the dark.

There is no wound you can see and no name written anywhere in this room. Whoever did all this did not write the name down. They knew it. They were not building a thing to be read; they were putting somebody somewhere good, and then shutting the door, and it did not occur to them that anyone would ever be standing where you are standing.

They are not going anywhere. Leave them be. The knife was left out on top for a reason.

A clay lamp with a black wick and no oil. A cup. A comb with two teeth gone. That is the whole of it, and it is the same list as half the things wedged into the cairn on the hill — a comb, a cup, small worthless objects carried a long way by somebody who meant something by them.

The old woman up there has been keeping the identical inventory for years without ever having seen this room. People do the same things. It turns out that is most of what there is to know about people.
